design_detail: Secondary analysis of the two-wave US National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (NESARC; Wave 1 2001-2002, Wave 2 2004-2005), using retrospective ages of onset to build discrete-time survival models of the transition from first use to DSM-IV dependence for four substances: nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine. Cumulative transition probabilities were estimated by the actuarial method overall and by racial and ethnic group, and predictors were estimated with univariable and stepwise multivariable discrete-time survival models with person-year as the unit of analysis.
can_establish: For US adults interviewed in both NESARC waves, the retrospectively reconstructed cumulative probability of meeting DSM-IV dependence criteria after first use of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine, the time from first use to dependence, differences between racial and ethnic groups, and which measured characteristics predict that transition.
cannot_establish: Anything specific to methamphetamine or amphetamines: this paper analyses only nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine, and stimulants appear only inside a composite 'any other substance use disorder' covariate. It also cannot establish causal ordering for time-varying predictors measured once, cannot correct recall of ages of onset decades earlier, and does not cover institutionalized populations.

sample.recruitment: National probability sample of the US civilian non-institutionalized population aged 18 and over living in households and group quarters (college quarters, group homes, boarding houses, non-transient hotels), with oversampling of Black and Hispanic respondents and of adults aged 18 to 24. Analysis is restricted to the subsamples reporting lifetime use of each substance.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: Wave 2 respondents reporting lifetime use of the substance in question (first full cigarette; at least one alcoholic drink not counting sips; any cannabis use; any cocaine or crack use). Excluded by the survey frame: institutionalized people, and at Wave 2 those who had died (n=1403), were deported or physically or mentally impaired (n=781) or were on active military duty (n=950).
sample.demographics: Weighted use prevalences by group are given in Table 1 (for example cocaine use reported by 9.0% of men and 4.8% of women; 7.5% of White, 4.2% of Black, 6.0% of Hispanic, 3.4% of Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander and 10.4% of American Indian or Alaska Native respondents). Age, urbanicity, nativity, education, individual and family income, marital status and employment are tabulated for each substance.
sample.attrition: Of 43,093 Wave 1 respondents, 34,653 were re-interviewed at Wave 2 (80.4%, editors' calculation). Weights adjust for Wave 2 non-response; the authors report that after weighting there were no significant differences between Wave 2 respondents and the eligible target population on Wave 1 sociodemographics or on any lifetime substance, mood, anxiety or personality disorder.
sample.selection_effects: Survivor and participation bias: people who died, were institutionalized or were too impaired to be interviewed between waves are excluded, and the authors note that institutionalized people have higher rates of dependence, so transition probabilities are likely underestimated. Ages of onset for both use and dependence are recalled retrospectively, in some cases decades later, by people whose recall may be affected by the drug use being reported.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in the AUDADIS-IV structured diagnostic interview: age at first full cigarette, first alcoholic drink, first cannabis use and first cocaine or crack use. No biological verification. The authors cite test-retest reliability of kappa 0.54 to 0.91 for AUDADIS-IV substance use disorder diagnoses.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed. The exposure is any lifetime use and its age of onset; quantity, frequency, route and continuity of use are not modelled. The authors list intermittent rather than continuous use as a limitation that makes the time from onset to dependence imprecise.
exposure.polysubstance: Handled as covariates: dependence on each of the other three index substances, and a composite 'any lifetime substance use disorder' covering the ten AUDADIS-IV classes (sedatives, tranquilizers, painkillers, stimulants, cannabis, cocaine or crack, hallucinogens, inhalants or solvents, heroin, other) plus alcohol and nicotine, excluding the substance under analysis. The paper reports that about half of nicotine users, a third of alcohol users, 80% of cannabis users and 93% of cocaine users had another substance use disorder (editors' calculation from Table 2).

comparison.controls: Within each substance, people who used it but had not (yet) become dependent, with person-years censored at the Wave 2 interview; and, for the racial and ethnic comparisons, White users as the reference group.
comparison.matching: None. Adjustment by multivariable discrete-time survival models with stepwise selection by likelihood-ratio test, so the covariate set differs between substances (the cocaine model retains no age or sex term, for example).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Pre-use characteristics are largely unmeasured or measured only as lifetime diagnoses without dates, so most psychiatric covariates cannot be placed before or after the start of use. Education, marital status and mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders were entered as time-dependent; income could not be, which the authors name as a limitation for interpreting racial and ethnic differences.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Other substance use is adjusted for rather than excluded; comparison groups include people using other drugs.

outcomes.instruments: AUDADIS-IV (Wave 2 version) computer algorithms for DSM-IV dependence (3 or more of 7 criteria in a 12-month period) for each substance; DSM-IV mood, anxiety, psychotic, conduct and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorders and personality disorders, with reported test-retest reliability of kappa 0.40 to 0.77 and good to excellent convergent validity. Family history of substance use disorder among first-degree relatives and early onset (before age 14) were self-reported.
outcomes.validity_norms: Reliability and validity evidence is cited for the instrument; all outcomes are retrospective self-report, and dependence is DSM-IV, not DSM-5 use disorder, so the figures are not interchangeable with DSM-5 use-disorder prevalences.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Transition' is the appearance of DSM-IV dependence at any age after the age of first use, in person-year survival time. Cumulative probability is the actuarial estimate at 1 year, 10 years and lifetime (that is, the end of the observed curve, which the paper describes as the probability of becoming dependent 'at some time in their life').
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Four substances, each with lifetime and interval probabilities, five racial and ethnic strata with log-rank tests, and univariable and multivariable models over roughly 20 covariates; stepwise selection was used, which further inflates the chance of spurious retained predictors.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; lay-interviewer structured interview with computer-generated diagnoses.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cumulative probability of transition to dependence: nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%, cannabis 8.9% lifetime; at one decade after first use, nicotine 15.6%, cocaine 14.8%, alcohol 11.0%, cannabis 5.9%; within the first year, about 2% for nicotine, alcohol and cannabis and 7.1% for cocaine. Median time from first use to dependence: nicotine about 27 years, alcohol 13, cannabis 5, cocaine 4. By racial and ethnic group (lifetime): nicotine 64.1% White, 70.7% Black, 64.7% Hispanic, 64.5% Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander, 85.1% American Indian or Alaska Native (log-rank 41.53, p<0.01); alcohol 22.6%, 21.4%, 26.7%, 16.9%, 29.0% (log-rank 47.16, p<0.01); cannabis 8.2%, 9.7%, 10.0%, 15.9%, 14.8% (log-rank 17.57, p<0.01); cocaine 16.8%, 35.9%, 20.5%, 20.3%, 22.5% (log-rank 30.40, p<0.01). Adjusted hazard ratios (Table 4) include, for cocaine dependence: Black versus White users 3.45 (2.2-5.3); mood disorder 2.58 (1.5-4.4); personality disorder 1.99 (1.4-2.9); alcohol dependence 2.56 (1.7-3.8); cannabis dependence 3.84 (1.8-8.2); onset before age 14, 0.34 (0.1-0.9). For cannabis dependence: male sex 1.44 (1.1-1.9); age 18 to 29 versus 45 and over 3.09 (1.9-4.9); mood disorder 2.69 (1.9-3.9); cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3-7.6); onset before 14, 0.63 (0.5-0.9). For nicotine dependence: age 18 to 29, 15.78 (13.9-17.9); anxiety disorder 1.96 (1.8-2.2); alcohol dependence 2.35 (2.1-2.6). No confidence interval is given for any cumulative probability.
analysis.covariates: Sex, age group, race and ethnicity, urbanicity, nativity, education, individual and family income, marital status, employment, mood, anxiety, personality, conduct, psychotic and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorders, dependence on each of the other three substances, family history of substance use disorder and onset before age 14; education, marital status and mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders entered as time-dependent. Stepwise selection means the final models differ by substance.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Secondary analysis of an existing survey; no protocol or analysis plan referenced.
analysis.selective_reporting: Characteristics of the people who became dependent are in supplementary tables (not read). Stepwise selection leaves several covariates absent from some columns of Table 4 without the non-significant estimates being shown. No intervals are reported for the cumulative probabilities, which are the paper's most-cited numbers.
analysis.power: Not discussed. Precision varies greatly by cell: the cocaine dependence model rests on 376 cases, the cannabis model on 529, and some subgroup cells are very small (only 51 cocaine users reported first use before age 14, yet an adjusted hazard ratio of 0.34 for that variable is reported).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among US adults who had ever used each substance, the retrospectively estimated lifetime probability of DSM-IV dependence was 67.5% for nicotine, 22.7% for alcohol, 20.9% for cocaine and 8.9% for cannabis, with dependence appearing fastest after cocaine and cannabis use. Transition probabilities differed by racial and ethnic group, most sharply for cocaine (35.9% in Black users versus 16.8% in White users). Psychiatric disorders, other substance dependence, family history and some sociodemographic factors predicted transition across substances. Early onset predicted transition in unadjusted models but reversed direction for cannabis and cocaine after adjustment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The paper's conclusions stay close to its data. The relevant gap is one of scope rather than overreach: it is routinely cited for the conditional probability of dependence given use, and it provides no estimate for methamphetamine or any amphetamine. A further gap is that the discussion explains racial and ethnic differences in transition with mechanisms (acculturative stress, discrimination, social capital, genetics) that the study did not measure, while the authors themselves note that income could not be modelled over time; and lifetime cumulative probabilities from actuarial curves are presented without intervals, although they project beyond the observed follow-up of many respondents.

timeline.event: Anthony, Warner and Kessler estimate dependence given use from the National Comorbidity Survey, including an estimate for stimulants, which is the usual source for amphetamine-type figures
Wagner and Anthony estimate 12% to 13% alcohol, 8% cannabis and 15% to 16% cocaine dependence within a decade of first use (cited in this paper's introduction and discussion as the comparison).
This study: NESARC two-wave estimates for nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine.

replication.where_it_stands: The decade-level estimates agree closely with the earlier National Comorbidity Survey work for alcohol, cannabis and cocaine, which is a genuine replication across two independent national surveys with different instruments. For methamphetamine the question remains open in this literature: the encyclopedia's conditional-probability figure for amphetamine-type stimulants must come from another source (Anthony et al., 1994 for stimulants, or a NESARC analysis of the stimulant category), not from this paper.

funding.funder: Not reported in the PMC author manuscript: it contains no funding statement, acknowledgements or role-of-funding-source section. One author is at the Laboratory of Epidemiology and Biometry, Division of Intramural Clinical and Biological Research, National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA), the agency that conducts NESARC, and is the corresponding author.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in this version of the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors at the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University (Department of Psychiatry and Mailman School of Public Health), Hospital de la Santa Creu i Sant Pau (Barcelona) and NIAAA. The survey's custodian agency is represented among the authors.

what_would_settle_it: For the encyclopedia's purpose, an equivalent analysis of the NESARC or NSDUH stimulant and methamphetamine categories, with prospective or at least repeated measurement of use frequency and route, would give a conditional probability of dependence after first methamphetamine use; more generally, a prospective cohort followed from before first use would remove the recall and survivor bias in all of these retrospective estimates.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: National probability frame for US civilian non-institutionalized adults, with Black, Hispanic and young adults oversampled; institutionalized people, who have higher dependence rates, are excluded, as the authors note.
Multistage probability sample with design-based analysis (Taylor series linearization in SUDAAN) and Wave 2 weights.
Large overall, but the cocaine (376 dependence cases) and cannabis (529) models and several racial and ethnic cells are small; the cell for cocaine use before age 14 contains 51 people.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Tables 1 and 2 describe sociodemographic, psychiatric and substance-use characteristics for each substance subsample, although their row totals do not match the stated subsample sizes (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 80.4% of Wave 1 respondents were re-interviewed (editors' calculation); weights adjust for non-response and the authors report no significant differences between respondents and the eligible target population on baseline measures.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: AUDADIS-IV with documented reliability and validity, but entirely self-report with no biological or record verification, and ages of onset are recalled retrospectively, in some cases across decades, by people whose recall may be affected by their drug use (a limitation the authors state).

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same structured instrument and computer algorithms for all respondents; dependence is DSM-IV throughout.

Actuarial survival estimation and discrete-time survival models with time-dependent covariates are appropriate for onset data, but cumulative probabilities are reported without confidence intervals, stepwise selection makes the models non-comparable across substances and inflates selection on chance, and no multiplicity adjustment is applied.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: Wave 2 retention is good and weighted, but the cumulative Wave 1 and Wave 2 response is lower than the retention figure alone suggests, and people who died or became too impaired between waves are necessarily excluded (survivor bias in a dependence-outcome analysis).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-conducted secondary analysis of a large national probability survey with a validated instrument and an appropriate survival framework. The limits on its numbers are structural rather than procedural: retrospective recall of ages of onset, exclusion of institutionalized and deceased people, lifetime cumulative probabilities projected without intervals, and stepwise model selection. For this encyclopedia the decisive point is not bias but scope: the paper contains no methamphetamine or amphetamine estimate, so it cannot support any claim about methamphetamine dependence liability.

key_findings.finding: The paper analyses only four substances, nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine. Methamphetamine and amphetamines are never an exposure or outcome; 'stimulants' appear only as one of the ten AUDADIS-IV classes making up a composite 'any other substance use disorder' covariate. No methamphetamine-specific conditional probability of dependence can be taken from this paper.
key_findings.locator: Title and Abstract; Methods › 2.3.1 Substance use and dependence; Table 2 footnote a
key_findings.note: Recorded explicitly because this reference is commonly cited for dependence-given-use figures across drugs.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime cumulative probability of transition from first use to DSM-IV dependence: nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%, cannabis 8.9%. No confidence intervals are given.

Cumulative probability of dependence one decade after first use: nicotine 15.6%, cocaine 14.8%, alcohol 11.0%, cannabis 5.9%. Within the first year of use: about 2% for nicotine, alcohol and cannabis, and 7.1% for cocaine.
Median time from first use to dependence: about 27 years for nicotine, 13 for alcohol, 5 for cannabis and 4 for cocaine.
key_findings.note: The subgroup medians in section 3.3.2 and 3.3.4 (8 years for alcohol and 2 years for cocaine among White users, who are the largest group) do not sit easily with these overall values; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Cocaine showed the largest racial and ethnic difference: lifetime transition to dependence in 35.9% of Black users versus 16.8% of White users, 20.5% of Hispanic, 20.3% of Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander and 22.5% of American Indian or Alaska Native users (log-rank 30.40, p<0.01). In the adjusted model, Black cocaine users had a hazard ratio of 3.45 (95% CI 2.2 to 5.3) versus White users.

Transition to nicotine dependence was highest among American Indian or Alaska Native users (85.1% versus 64.1% in White users; log-rank 41.53, p<0.01); for alcohol the range was 16.9% (Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander) to 29.0% (American Indian or Alaska Native); for cannabis 8.2% (White) to 15.9% (Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander).

Psychiatric comorbidity predicted transition for every substance in adjusted models: mood disorder hazard ratios 1.62 (nicotine), 2.29 (alcohol), 2.69 (cannabis), 2.58 (cocaine); personality disorder 1.42, 1.64, 2.30, 1.99; anxiety disorder 1.96, 1.98, 2.31 (not retained for cocaine).

Dependence on another substance strongly predicted transition: for example cannabis dependence predicted cocaine dependence (hazard ratio 3.84, 1.8 to 8.2) and cocaine dependence predicted cannabis dependence (4.14, 2.3 to 7.6); alcohol dependence predicted nicotine (2.35), cannabis (2.55) and cocaine (2.56) dependence.

Early onset (before age 14) predicted transition in unadjusted models (cannabis 2.47, cocaine 1.65 non-significant, nicotine 1.29, alcohol 2.51) but reversed direction after adjustment for cannabis (0.63, 0.5 to 0.9) and cocaine (0.34, 0.1 to 0.9), while remaining positive for nicotine (1.13). The authors interpret this as early onset being a marker of concomitant psychiatric and substance comorbidity rather than a risk factor in itself.
key_findings.note: Only 51 cocaine users reported first use before age 14 (Table 2), so the adjusted estimate of 0.34 rests on a very small cell.

key_findings.finding: Co-occurring substance use disorders were the norm among users of the illicit substances: about 51% of nicotine users, 31% of alcohol users, 81% of cannabis users and 93% of cocaine users had a substance use disorder involving another substance (editors' calculation from Table 2 counts; the discussion states one third, half, more than 80% and 90%).

Sample: 43,093 Wave 1 respondents, 34,653 re-interviewed at Wave 2 (80.4%, editors' calculation); analyses use the subsamples reporting lifetime use of each substance (stated as 15,918 nicotine, 28,907 alcohol, 7,389 cannabis, 2,259 cocaine), with DSM-IV diagnoses generated by AUDADIS-IV algorithms and all estimates weighted to the US population.
key_findings.locator: Methods › 2.1 Sample and procedures; 2.2 Data collection

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: self-report without objective confirmation; recall bias increasing with the interval since the event and with drug-related cognitive impairment; intermittent rather than continuous use making the time from onset to dependence imprecise; exclusion of institutionalized people, who have higher dependence rates; and the impossibility of modelling income as a time-dependent covariate.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, last paragraph before the summary

reporting_issues.issue: The row totals in Table 1 do not match the subsample sizes stated in the abstract and methods. Every stratification in Table 1 sums to 16,053 for nicotine, 29,160 for alcohol, 7,409 for cannabis and 2,263 for cocaine, while the stated subsamples are 15,918, 28,907, 7,389 and 2,259 (arithmetic by the editors, consistent across gender, age, race, urbanicity, nativity, education and employment).
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominators of the descriptive table are internally consistent but differ from the analytic Ns by 135, 253, 20 and 4 people. The percentages quoted in the discussion for co-occurring substance use disorders reproduce the Table 1 denominators, so the larger figures appear to be the actual subsample sizes.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the counts for 'any lifetime psychiatric disorder' are identical to those for 'any lifetime mood disorder' (for example 11,458 and 4,595 for nicotine; 4,573 and 2,836 for cannabis) while the accompanying percentages differ sharply (nicotine 27.4% versus 44.5% in the 'no' rows, cannabis 5.1% versus 17.7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two rows cannot both be right: the number of people with no psychiatric disorder of any kind cannot equal the number with no mood disorder. One set of counts or percentages has been mis-transcribed, so Table 2's psychiatric rows should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of dependence cases in Tables 3 and 4 (7,320 nicotine, 4,822 alcohol, 529 cannabis, 376 cocaine) is lower than the number of people with each lifetime dependence diagnosis in Table 2 (7,473, 4,869, 564, 398), with no explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Between 2% and 6% of dependence cases are missing from the survival models, presumably for missing onset ages; the exclusion is not described or characterized.

reporting_issues.issue: The overall median latency to dependence (13 years for alcohol, 4 for cocaine) is longer than the median reported for White users, who are the largest group in each subsample (8 years for alcohol, 2 years for cocaine).
reporting_issues.consequence: An overall median should normally lie near that of the dominant group; either the overall and subgroup medians come from differently specified curves or one set is misreported. Latency figures should be cited with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.1 states that 'rates of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and alcohol use were higher among males', listing alcohol twice where cocaine is meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the table shows the intended comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints an individual-income cell for nicotine users as '44.o' instead of 44.0.
No confidence intervals are given for any cumulative transition probability, including the headline lifetime figures of 67.5%, 22.7%, 20.9% and 8.9%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The precision of the most-cited numbers in the paper cannot be assessed, and lifetime estimates from actuarial curves extrapolate beyond the follow-up observed for younger respondents.

reporting_issues.issue: Multivariable models were built by stepwise selection, so covariates appear in some substance columns of Table 4 and not others (the cocaine model retains neither sex nor age group), and the non-selected estimates are not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's claim that predictors are shared across substances is partly an artefact of which variables survived selection in each model; the columns of Table 4 are not directly comparable.

reporting_issues.issue: The PMC author manuscript carries no funding statement, acknowledgements or conflict-of-interest declaration.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding and interests cannot be recorded from this version; the published version or the journal page would be needed.
